title: Altona: refuge and freedom of worship

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Dutch Mennonite refugees established a congregation at Altona under privileges that protected worship and trade.
paragraphs: Mennonite refugees from the Netherlands found an opening at Altona, outside the restrictions of neighboring Hamburg. In 1601 the rulers of Holstein-Pinneberg granted religious and commercial privileges to Mennonites and Reformed refugees. The Mennonite congregation first worshiped in private homes; its later meetinghouse on the Große Freiheit became a lasting sign of this refuge.

The surviving privilege of 6 June 1641 renewed protection for Mennonites who had lived there for forty years. It recognized religious freedom and trade while requiring peaceful conduct and obedience to the law. The congregation’s story therefore joins freedom of conscience to the everyday work of establishing households and livelihoods.

The chart summarizes this development as admission to citizenship in 1601. The documentary record gives the more specific language of settlement, worship, and commercial privileges. Those protections helped sustain a Dutch-speaking Mennonite community through changing local rulers and circumstances.

title: Christian Funk and the Revolutionary-era separation

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: A disagreement over allegiance and support for the American Revolution divided Pennsylvania Mennonites and left a long search for reconciliation.
paragraphs: Christian Funk was a bishop in the Franconia fellowship in Pennsylvania. During the American Revolution he supported accepting the new government and contributing toward its cause. Other Mennonite leaders believed these steps compromised their peace convictions and refusal of political oaths. The dispute led to the separation remembered as the Funkite division of 1778–1779.

The division endured after the war. Attempts at reconciliation in 1804 and 1806 turned on whether Funk must acknowledge wrongdoing and whether the ministers ordained within his group would be recognized. His own memoir, Mirror for All Mankind, records his understanding of the conflict and forms part of the evidence preserved by the Mennonite Heritage Center.

The separate congregations gradually diminished after Funk’s death in 1811, with members joining other local churches. The Heritage Center records a final communion in 1851 at the Franconia meetinghouse. This explains the chart’s approximate ending around 1850 without turning a gradual dissolution into a single universal date.

title: Allianz fellowship in Molotschna

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Bible courses and open fellowship on Mennonite estates contributed to the Allianz-related church organized in 1905.
paragraphs: At the end of the nineteenth century, Mennonites from southern Russia attended evangelical gatherings at Blankenburg in Germany. Peter P. Schmidt and David J. Dick brought these contacts into the Molotschna setting by sponsoring Bible courses on their estates. Mennonite Brethren and other Mennonite teachers, ministers, and families met for study, preaching, and fellowship.

The gatherings continued into the next decade and included celebrations of communion among believers from different church backgrounds. In 1905 an Allianz-oriented group organized as the Evangelische Mennonitische Brüderschaft, also known as Evangelische Mennoniten Gemeinden. The name described this particular movement in Ukraine rather than every organization later abbreviated EMB.

Peter Schmidt’s notebooks and the families’ guest registers preserve dates of meetings, visiting speakers, and personal reflections. Their archival record gives the chart’s brief 1905 marker a setting in households, Scripture study, and the movement of people between European evangelical circles and Mennonite congregations.

title: Mennonite Board of Guardians: helping immigrants

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Two Mennonite aid committees united to help families travel from the Russian Empire and establish new homes in North America.
paragraphs: The Mennonite Board of Guardians was organized at Summerfield, Illinois, on 2 December 1873. It brought together committees formed by the Indiana–Michigan Mennonite Conference and the Western District of the General Conference. Christian Krehbiel served as president, David Goerz as secretary, John F. Funk as treasurer, and Bernhard Warkentin as an immigration agent.

The board negotiated with railway and steamship companies and raised gifts and loans to help families who could not afford passage. Its work soon extended beyond transport to settlement assistance, including cooperation with relief efforts in Kansas. This was shared practical service across conference boundaries during a major migration.

Most of the initial work was accomplished by the end of 1875, although settlement aid and loan repayments continued afterward. The chart prints the board twice on different lines; both markers refer here to the same cooperative organization, rather than two unrelated bodies founded in the same year.

title: Canadian Mennonite Board of Colonization

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Canadian Mennonites organized relief and immigration assistance for families affected by revolution, famine, and displacement.
paragraphs: Representatives from Mennonite communities in western Canada met at Regina on 18 October 1920 to coordinate relief for people suffering in the former Russian Empire. Their work developed into a specific immigration organization, the Canadian Mennonite Board of Colonization, established in 1922 under the leadership of David Toews and A. A. Friesen.

The board negotiated with the Canadian government and the Canadian Pacific Railway so refugees could travel on credit. The first immigrants arrived in July 1923. Over the following years, established Mennonite households welcomed newcomers while the board helped arrange transport, settlement, and repayment of travel costs.

The archival fonds preserves registration forms, correspondence, minutes, and later relief and immigration records. It distinguishes the 1920 relief initiative from the 1922 board organization, clarifying the chart’s earlier date. The records also trace renewed immigration work after the Second World War and later cooperation that contributed to MCC Canada.

title: The Dutch Gemeentedag movement

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Dutch Mennonite gatherings and brotherhood houses grew from a desire to renew shared spiritual life.
paragraphs: Contacts with the Quakers at Woodbrooke in England and the Woodbrookers at Barchem helped inspire Dutch Mennonites to organize the Gemeentedagbeweging in 1917. The movement created gatherings where believers from different congregations could meet for spiritual reflection, fellowship, and the strengthening of Christian life.

The first national Gemeentedag met at Utrecht in August 1917. Further gatherings and camps followed, including meetings at Giethoorn. The desire for places where young and old could share this life contributed to brotherhood houses; Fredeshiem opened as a Frisian Mennonite center in 1929.

Fredeshiem’s own institutional history explicitly identifies the Quaker connection and the 1917 movement. It therefore supplies a documented name and setting for the chart’s small, partly unreadable reference to Quaker-inspired renewal. The movement belonged within Dutch Mennonite life and did not represent a new sixteenth-century branch.

title: International Mennonite Peace Committee

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Mennonites organized international cooperation to support conscientious objectors and strengthen their peace witness.
paragraphs: Immediately after the Mennonite World Conference meetings at Amsterdam and Elspeet in 1936, a smaller gathering organized the International Mennonite Peace Committee. The committee sought to encourage the peace convictions of Mennonites and support those who faced difficulties because they refused military service.

The organizational meeting was held at Fredeshiem on 4 July 1936, with Jacob ter Meulen serving as executive secretary. Its work connected the confession of nonresistance with assistance to people under political pressure. War interrupted the early organization, and international cooperation had to be rebuilt after 1945.

A reorganized committee met in 1949 with representatives from European and North American Mennonite communities. Mennonite World Conference’s own historical account places this initiative within the development of shared global witness. The independently documented dates give substance to the chart’s peace-committee marker without guessing its tiny printed digits.

title: Early Mennonite Sunday schools in Ontario

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Congregations in Waterloo County introduced organized Sunday instruction alongside the worshiping life of the church.
paragraphs: The Wanner and Bechtel, or Hagey, meetinghouses in Waterloo County, Ontario, began Sunday schools in 1840. Mennonite historical accounts identify these among the earliest such schools in North America. A school at Berlin, later Kitchener, followed in 1841, and further examples appeared in Pennsylvania and elsewhere.

Sunday instruction provided an organized setting for learning Scripture and passing on the faith. Its introduction also raised questions about appropriate teachers, methods, and the place of a new educational structure within congregational life. Later Mennonite conferences did not all respond in the same way to these innovations.

The chart’s 1840 marker belongs to this local development rather than to the beginning of Christian teaching among Mennonites. The history is connected with the later debates over Sunday schools and revival meetings that shaped Old Order and conference relationships, while keeping the first Waterloo-area schools in their own setting.

title: Oberholtzer and the Eastern District Conference

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: A Pennsylvania division over conference order and cooperation produced the fellowship later known as Eastern District Conference.
paragraphs: John H. Oberholtzer and other ministers sought a written conference constitution and changes in the way their Pennsylvania fellowship conducted its work. Conflict with the Franconia leadership led to a separation in 1847 and the organization of the East Pennsylvania Conference. Surviving conference minutes begin in that year.

The new fellowship promoted cooperation in education, publishing, and mission and became part of the General Conference Mennonite Church. Its congregations formed what became known as the Eastern District Conference. The chart’s later 1863 marker must be read within this developing conference history; it does not replace the documented 1847 beginning.

The conference’s minutes, correspondence, and ministerial records preserve both the practical work and the disagreements behind the division. Much later, Eastern District and Franconia reconciled and formed Mosaic Mennonite Conference in 2019. The institutional history presents that reunion as a continuation of a long shared story.

title: The Masontown meetings of 1872

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: Daniel Brenneman and John F. Funk conducted a series of meetings that became an early milestone in Mennonite Church revivalism.
paragraphs: In 1872 Daniel Brenneman, assisted by John F. Funk, held revival meetings at Masontown, Pennsylvania. Mennonite histories identify these as the first such series within the Mennonite Church body commonly abbreviated MC. This is a claim about that particular revival-meeting form and church setting, not about the beginning of Anabaptist evangelism.

A series of meetings extended preaching and invitation beyond the usual congregational service. Advocates hoped to awaken faith and call hearers to conversion and renewed Christian life. Other Mennonites questioned the new methods, contributing to the wider nineteenth-century discussion of worship, discipline, and innovations.

Later evangelists, including John S. Coffman, carried the revival emphasis into further congregations. The Masontown marker is therefore linked here with the stories of Funk and the regional Old Order divisions, while each development retains its own dates and causes.

title: The Evangelical United Mennonite conference of 1882

date.basis: The primary minutes date the meeting to 4–7 October 1882. The body formed in 1879; the chart’s abbreviated label is not independent evidence of an 1882 founding.

summary: Preserved minutes document an 1882 conference concerned with ministry, publishing, mission, and common church discipline.
paragraphs: The first General Conference of the Evangelical United Mennonites met at Bethel in Elkhart County, Indiana, on 4–7 October 1882. Delegates came from Ontario, Indiana and Michigan, and Pennsylvania, with representatives of the church’s printing work. Solomon Eby chaired the gathering, and English and German secretaries recorded its business.

The conference recommended courses of reading for prospective ministers, including Scripture and Menno Simons’s writings. It arranged support for mission work in Kansas, appointed leaders for the printing establishment, and considered relationships with the Brethren in Christ. Its resolutions also addressed worship and the conduct expected of church members.

The Evangelical United Mennonites had already formed through a merger in 1879. The 1882 minutes document a meeting of that existing body, not its founding. They provide a named, dated conference to read alongside the chart’s abbreviated evangelical-conference label, whose exact intended identification is not proven. This history leads toward the Mennonite Brethren in Christ, distinct from the Canadian Evangelical Mennonite Conference that later developed from Kleine Gemeinde.

title: Roxbury Holiness Camp and Brethren in Christ renewal

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: A series of revival meetings in Pennsylvania developed into a continuing place of worship, Bible teaching, and fellowship.
paragraphs: Roxbury’s institutional history dates its beginnings to revival meetings held in an old dance hall in 1935. These gatherings became the Roxbury Holiness Camp Meeting. The chart places Roxbury among the 1930s developments through which the Brethren in Christ shared the holiness emphasis.

The camp offered an extended setting for preaching, prayer, music, Bible teaching, and fellowship across local congregations. Brethren in Christ accounts remember the participation of teachers such as O. B. Ulery and the importance of annual gatherings for families. The camp thus became part of a network of worship and renewal rather than a new denomination.

Over time the grounds developed beyond the summer meeting into a year-round setting for retreats and ministry. This account uses the camp’s specific 1935 historical statement for the initiating revival meetings, while retaining the chart’s broader 1930s setting for the spread of camp-meeting life.

title: The Lone Tree conference and confession

date.basis: Date or period documented in the cited institutional, archival, or historical source; source-chart wording remains separately inventoried.

summary: The Church of God in Christ, Mennonite gathered at Lone Tree, Kansas, and recorded a common confession of faith.
paragraphs: The General Conference of the Church of God in Christ, Mennonite met at the Lone Tree congregation near Moundridge, Kansas, on 23–26 November 1896. John Holdeman served as moderator. The preserved Articles of Confession identify the meeting, its place, and its date, providing a documentary anchor for the chart’s small Lone Tree label.

The conference belonged to a church movement that had begun in Ohio in 1859 and later gathered members across wider regions. Meeting together allowed congregations to express shared teaching and address common church life. The confession forms part of that movement’s written record alongside Holdeman’s preaching and other publications.

Lone Tree is therefore presented as a conference milestone within the existing church history, not as the beginning of a separate denomination. The date is established from the surviving document; the indistinct date digits in the supplied photograph are left as a source-legibility question.

title: Reading the chart’s worldwide reach
summary: The source map records a widening geographical horizon while leaving individual local histories to their own documented timelines.
paragraphs: The lower map on the supplied timeline carries lines and place labels across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Pacific. Its purpose is to show that the church history extends beyond the European beginnings and North American migrations displayed in the main branches. The map includes both countries with long-established communities and places associated with later mission work.

These labels do not themselves supply founding dates or identify every local congregation and believer. This archive therefore keeps the map as a guide to geographical scope rather than turning the position of a line into a dated church genealogy. The histories of migration, MCC service, mission, and Mennonite World Conference provide documented starting points for following that wider story.

Historical names and spellings in the chart remain part of its record. Local church archives and named firsthand accounts can add the people, languages, congregations, and events that a world map cannot contain. In particular, unnamed local participants are not replaced with invented biographies.
